issues.legal_issue: A suit seeking only an injunction is not an adequate remedy where possession of a vacant site depends on resolving a serious and complex dispute over title and identification of the property.
material_facts: The plaintiff claimed the disputed property under a registered assignment deed and sought an injunction based on his alleged possession.
The defendant disputed the plaintiff’s title and possession, asserting that the property belonged to his family and was not included in the plaintiff’s deed or purchase certificate.

The parties’ descriptions and survey numbers did not clearly identify the disputed property, and the lower courts’ findings relied on a disputed boundary and an inference of possession from an adjoining plot.
The property was a vacant site, so determining de jure possession depended on resolving title; the Court considered that the documentary and oral evidence would require a full trial.
After the High Court remanded the suit, the plaintiff amended the pleadings to seek a declaration of title, and the defendant amended the written statement in response.
issues.conclusion: The bare-injunction suit was not an appropriate vehicle for deciding possession without resolving the serious and complex title dispute. The parties should have their title rights adjudicated in the comprehensive declaratory proceedings, and the High Court’s remand was not disturbed because the pleadings had been amended to seek a declaration of title.
issues.legal_principle: Under Anathula Sudhakar v. P. Buchi Reddy (2008) 4 SCC 594, a suit for injunction simpliciter ordinarily turns on possession, but where a vacant site makes de jure possession dependent on title, title may directly and substantially arise. A court should not decide title in an injunction suit where title is seriously disputed and the matter involves complicated questions of fact and law; the remedy is a comprehensive suit for declaration of title. Although a court may decide a simple and straightforward title issue in an injunction suit where there are necessary pleadings and an appropriate issue, that is an exception. Jharkhand State Housing Board v. Didar Singh, (2019) 17 SCC 692, likewise recognizes that a bare injunction is inadequate when a genuine dispute creates a cloud over title. Here the title and identification disputes were complex, and the plaintiff had amended the suit to seek declaratory relief.

rule.if: bare_injunction_suit and vacant_site and (serious_title_dispute and property_identification_disputed) and possession_depends_on_title and title_issue_requires_full_trial

predicates.bare_injunction_suit: The claimant brought a suit seeking an injunction without initially seeking a declaration of title.
predicates.vacant_site: The disputed property was a vacant site.
predicates.serious_title_dispute: The opposing party asserted a competing claim of ownership that seriously placed the claimant’s title in dispute.
predicates.property_identification_disputed: The parties disputed whether the property claimed by the claimant was the same property described or identified in the evidence.
predicates.possession_depends_on_title: Determining possession of the property required establishing which party had title to it.
predicates.title_issue_requires_full_trial: Resolving title required consideration of complicated factual or legal matters and a full assessment of documentary and oral evidence.

issues.definition: When a suit seeks only an injunction over a vacant site and serious disputes about title and identification make possession depend on a complex title determination, the output is that a declaration of title is required.
